title: SEPA: Europe’s unsung hero
author: European Central Bank
text:
THE ECB BLOGSEPA: Europe’s unsung hero3 November 2026By Elisabeth Beckmann, Justus Meyer and Katharina Allinger[1] The authors are grateful to the OeNB Euro Survey team for collecting the data underlying this analysis. Despite the expansion of the Single Euro Payments Area, or SEPA for short, many households continue to rely on costly channels for transferring money across borders in Europe. New survey evidence suggests that public awareness of European payment integration is still surprisingly limited.The Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) offers seamless cross-border payments between 41 European countries, but its silent success creates a paradox. Thanks to SEPA, many people don’t think about the service they use when making a money transfer. Yet many haven’t heard of SEPA at all. This all comes at a cost. Especially in countries, which have recently joined SEPA, or for migrant workers sending money back home, expensive alternative providers of cross-border payments are often still the first port of call.In this blog post, we look at six south-eastern European countries drawing on the OeNB Euro Survey to show why cross-border payments matter for households, how SEPA provides an inexpensive response to this need and how consumers can benefit from using it. Why cross-border payments matter for householdsEvery year, migrant workers across the euro area send billions of euro to support family members both in the European Union and in countries aspiring to join it. Bulgaria and Albania are good examples of two different aspects of remittance flows. In the case of Bulgaria – the newest member of the euro area – remittance inflows amount to almost €3 billion, illustrating the scale of the phenomenon in absolute terms. As for Albania, while inflows exceed €2.5 billion – somewhat lower in absolute terms – they are substantially more significant relative to the size of the economy and account for around 8.4% of GDP, compared with 2.1% in the case of Bulgaria. Remittance receipt is also widespread at the consumer level, with around one in five people in Albania (21%) and one in six in Bosnia and Herzegovina (17%) reporting receipt of remittances, compared with 10% in the Republic of North Macedonia, 9% in Serbia, 8% in Bulgaria and 4% in Romania.[2] Authors' calculations are based on the World Bank’s World Development Indicators, indicators of personal remittances, received (current US dollars) and personal remittances, received (percentage of GDP). Values in euro are converted from current US dollar figures and rounded. Data on the share of consumers receiving remittances is based on the OeNB Euro Survey autumn wave 2025; data are weighted. See also OeNB Blog "Remittances 101" part 1 and part 2. Even so, the formal banking system is still far from being the dominant channel for these payments.[3] In Bulgaria and Romania, 10-20% of transfers are reported as SEPA bank-based transfers (see Chart 1, turquoise bar). However, it is not possible to determine whether transfers reported as “through bank branches” also include SEPA transfers. For all other countries, the data do not allow firm conclusions on SEPA usage but show that the majority of transfers are non-SEPA. Across six countries in south-eastern Europe, around one-third of recipients receive money in cash via relatives or friends and another third through physical money transfer operators (Chart 1).[4] See also OeNB Blog "Remittances 101" part 1 and part 2. Bank-based remittance transfers generally include SEPA credit transfers when both sender and recipient institutions participate in SEPA. The differences between countries are considerable. Let’s take Bulgaria and Albania, two countries at different stages along the path to EU and euro area integration. While bank-based channels are more often used in Bulgaria, money transfer operators remain equally important. In Albania, more than half of recipients use money transfer operators. Many remittance senders also choose informal, cash-based channels.Chart 1Where payment integration is incomplete: reliance on non-bank and informal channels for remittance transfers(percentage of consumers)Source: The OeNB Euro Survey, authors’ calculations. Note: The chart shows population-weighted data for the distribution of remittance receipt channels in Bulgaria (BG), Romania (RO), Albania (AL), Bosnia and Herzegovina (BA), the Republic of North Macedonia (MK) and Serbia (RS). These choices can be costly. Depending on the countries involved, the provider and the payment channel, remittance fees can differ by more than 10 percentage points for the same transfer. Cash-to-cash transfers, where money is deposited and then withdrawn in cash, typically incur fees of around 6% to 12%. Even digital non-bank transfers can cost between 1.5% and 4.5%. In some cases, costs are substantially higher.[5] Authors’ calculations are based on the World Bank’s Remittance Prices Worldwide database. Reported fees refer to selected cash-to-cash and digital remittance channels in the Germany-Bulgaria, Spain-Romania and Italy-Albania corridors in the third quarter of 2025. Given the scale of remittance flows, these differences matter. A fee of 5% corresponds to around €140 million on annual remittance inflows to Bulgaria and around €130 million on those to Albania. Meanwhile, SEPA transfers are designed to make cross-border euro payments as simple and as inexpensive as domestic transfers. Unlike other options, using SEPA can mean more of the money sent reaches recipients, especially when these hold euro-denominated accounts and can therefore avoid currency conversion costs.[6] Not all consumers can immediately switch to SEPA-based transfers, as access requires participating payment service providers and typically a payment account. According to the OeNB Euro Survey, account ownership varies considerably across countries: around half of the population in Albania lack a current account or similar product, compared with 25% in Romania and 17% in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Account ownership is much lower in Bulgaria (10%), Serbia (8%) and the Republic of North Macedonia (2%). Europe’s answer to expensive cross-border paymentsSEPA is Europe's answer to costly and fragmented cross-border euro payments. Its objective is simple: a euro transfer from one participating country to another should be as easy and straightforward as a domestic payment. Before the creation of SEPA, cross-border euro transfers were often slower, involved different national standards and could attract significantly higher fees. SEPA replaced this fragmented landscape with common payment schemes and harmonised standards.Today, SEPA connects 41 countries. The list of participants includes not only all euro area countries but all those EU Member States not using the euro as their currency and, increasingly, EU candidate countries (those on the path to becoming EU Member States). While Bulgaria and Romania have been part of the SEPA geographical scope for more than 15 years, Albania and the Republic of North Macedonia joined in 2024 and Serbia in 2025, while Bosnia and Herzegovina officially applied for SEPA membership in August 2026. This has further expanded European payment integration into south-eastern Europe, where remittances play an important role for many households. The benefits for consumers do not materialise overnight, however, as simply becoming part of SEPA’s geographical scope does not immediately bring with it a fully operational payment system. Nevertheless, it represents an important step towards lower-cost, more transparent, reliable and integrated cross-border euro payments.A success story hidden in plain sightSEPA's success creates a paradox. The more seamlessly cross-border euro payments work, the less consumers need to think about the infrastructure behind them. SEPA’s functionality makes it largely invisible. Yet this also raises a question. Do households recognise the benefits brought by European payment integration? Survey data suggest that many do not (Chart 2). Despite SEPA being one of Europe’s most successful financial integration projects, fewer than 40% of consumers in the countries surveyed report having heard of it. Whether their country has been part of SEPA’s geographical scope for many years or joined only recently makes no difference. This is striking given the publicity surrounding recent expansions to include Albania, the Republic of North Macedonia and Serbia. By contrast, awareness of crypto-assets is much higher, although fewer than one in ten consumers own crypto-assets in any of the countries surveyed, with the highest ownership rate at only 6%.[7] Source: Authors' calculation based on the OeNB Euro Survey 2025. For comparable evidence regarding the euro area, see Zamora-Pérez, A. (2026), “Who owns crypto in the euro area? Drivers of crypto adoption, payment use, and its interaction with fiat cash”, Working Paper Series”, No 3215, ECB, April. Chart 2SEPA awareness lags behind awareness of crypto-assets across CESEE countries(percentage of consumers)Source: The OeNB Euro Survey authors’ calculations. Note: The chart shows population-weighted data for the share of consumers in Bulgaria (BG), the Czech Republic (CZ), Hungary (HU), Poland (PL), Romania (RO), Albania (AL), Bosnia and Herzegovina (BA), the Republic of North Macedonia (MK) and Serbia (RS) who have heard of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) and crypto assets. Still, one could argue that low recognition is not problematic. After all, low awareness does not necessarily imply low usage. Consumers may benefit from SEPA without knowing what the acronym stands for. However, persistently low awareness levels suggest that the benefits of European payment integration may not be equally important to all households.Indeed, awareness tends to be higher among consumers with higher incomes, higher educational attainment and stronger financial literacy. As Chart 3 shows, consumers with tertiary education are around 17 percentage points more likely to have heard of SEPA than those with only primary education. And, overall, financially literate consumers are substantially more likely to be aware of it. While it is difficult to quantify the full benefits of SEPA, a simple upper-bound calculation suggests that reducing remittance fees from current levels could save households tens or even hundreds of millions of euro every year. However, the benefits extend beyond transaction costs. Given that a substantial share of remittances are still transferred informally in cash, SEPA also offers gains in convenience, speed, reliability and security, reducing the need to rely on friends or relatives travelling across borders to deliver money.Chart 3SEPA awareness is closely linked to education and financial literacySource: The OeNB Euro Survey, authors’ calculations. Notes: Coefficients show the estimated effect of respondent characteristics on the probability of having heard of SEPA. Country fixed effects and labour market controls are included but not displayed. Positive coefficients indicate a higher likelihood of SEPA awareness relative to the reference category.From integration to consumer benefitsThese findings raise an important question. Since payment choices entail meaningful differences in costs, to what extent would consumers act differently if they were aware of the opportunities created by an integrated European payments market? While the survey evidence presented here cannot answer this question directly, evidence from a related information experiment suggests that awareness and consumer choice cannot be conflated. Providing households with information about deposit insurance guarantees might improve awareness but it has little effect on financial choices.[8] See Beckmann, E. and Meyer, J. (2026), “Saving in cash or saving at banks: The role of deposit insurance guarantees” (mimeo). So, greater awareness of SEPA alone may be insufficient to change payment behaviour. Yet when the cost of sending money across borders can differ substantially across channels, even small changes in payment choices may have tangible consequences for households. And the more people are aware of them, the greater the chance they will benefit. In any case, a better understanding of the benefits of SEPA and the related – almost free – payment services would have immediate concrete effects at least for one group: the workers sending money home across borders. Using SEPA payments instead of costly cash to cash services could save them quite a bit.
